interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between CMD and ENTRYPOINT in a Dockerfile?
interviewQuestions.answer: ENTRYPOINT specifies the immutable command or executable that will always run when the container starts. CMD provides default arguments to the ENTRYPOINT, which can be easily overridden by passing CLI arguments to 'docker run'.

interviewQuestions.question: How do Docker images utilize Copy-On-Write (CoW) filesystems?
interviewQuestions.answer: Docker image layers are strictly read-only. When a container runs, Docker attaches a thin, writable container layer on top using union filesystems (like overlay2). Any modification to an existing file copies the file from the lower read-only layer into the top writable layer, preserving image immutability and saving disk space.

interviewQuestions.question: What is the difference between a bind mount and a named volume?
interviewQuestions.answer: Bind mounts map an arbitrary file or directory from the host filesystem into the container, reliant on host directory structure and permissions (ideal for source code during local dev). Named volumes are managed entirely by Docker inside its storage directory (/var/lib/docker/volumes/), offering superior performance, portability, and backup capabilities (ideal for databases in production).

interviewQuestions.question: How do you minimize container security vulnerabilities in production?
interviewQuestions.answer: 1) Run as a non-root USER; 2) Use minimal base images like Distroless or Alpine; 3) Drop unnecessary Linux capabilities (--cap-drop=ALL); 4) Use multi-stage builds to avoid leaking compiler tools and secrets; 5) Scan images in CI/CD using Trivy; 6) Set the root filesystem to read-only (--read-only).
